messages.author: 9071f4fcea2a122e
messages.subject: Help! Best practices for deploying app
parts:
Hi everyone, 

I have no experience with SHINY development, yet I was tasked with developing SOP or best practices for deploying apps. This is the result of an individual within our organization making major changes to the app after the test deployment (instead of just fixing any bugs, which was what intended). This resulted in the app no longer working when deployed. For procedures, they are seeking something along these lines:

- Freeze all development and ensure app works on a local machine
- Deploy to production server 
- User testing and bug fixing
- all fixes must be submitted and tested in a local environment

They gave me the above lines as a guide for what to write.

Does anyone have a SOP or best practices for these procedures that they would be willing to share?

TIA!

GK04

messages.subject: Re: Help! Best practices for deploying app
parts:
My personal feeling is that Github (or a similar platform) has great features to help with this, especially if you hook it into a CI server as well.

If you manage all your code on with version control like Github, the only way to get your code from the "develop" branch (where work takes place) into the "master" branch (which is the live, deployed version) is to successfully complete a merge via a pull request. You can build as much structure around this process as you want. A typical workflow might be:
  1. User wants to work on a new feature.
  2. User creates a specific branch to contain changes to the code that relate to this feature.
  3. User finishes their work and is ready to get feedback and incorporate the new feature.
  4. User creates a pull request from their feature branch into develop
  5. Other users review their work, and give feedback. User can add more changes into the pull request until everyone is happy.
  6. The feature branch is merged into develop and the pull request is closed.
  7. When the group is ready to promote the current develop version to the live environment, a pull request is created that will merge the develop branch into the master branch.
  8. After any feedback and corrections, the group is happy that develop is safe to deploy live, and the merge is completed and the pull request is closed. Live now incorporates User's new feature.
This is a very long-winded description of the formal code management practice; it needn't be a very time-consuming process if the feedback rounds are fast. This process can be used for anything from 2 people working on a presentation to hundreds of people working on Youtube's back-end code. This process avoids the situation where changes get pushed live without anyone noticing. In the event of catastrophe, the version control system allows you to roll back to a previous version very easily.

Another major advantage of using tools for this is that many steps can be automated. You can set up a Continuous Integration server that will validate every single commit and pull request by running scripts or processes you define. For work on an R package this might be running R CMD Check and then Building the package. For a shiny dashboard, it could be successfully passing unit tests defined with the testthat package. If you have a rule that no pull request can be merged if its tests are failing, and your tests are set up well, then you ensure that no code that causes breaking changes slips through the net and gets merged by accident. If that ever does happen, you can improve your tests to stop it happening again.

Finally, you can set up automated deployment. You can have your CI server, or some other service, monitor the master branch constantly for updates. As soon as you merge that PR into master, the service will update the server for you without you having to do anything manually. You can roll back just by reverting the master branch. You can have other environments set up to track other branches - a development environment tracking develop, a specific QA/UAT environment tracking a particular branch, and even environments set to track specific feature branches if you want. With everything being automatically tested and then deployed if the tests pass, you can speed up your development processes a lot.

There is tons of advice, training, books, courses, and much more about these sorts of processes. Developing a shiny project is no different to any other software project in these things, so you can use the tools that are already available to you. I hope this helped :)
